Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-07 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-2026-07-07-0a1b2c3d (placeholder)

Summary:
Quick hosted API sandbox onboarding focused on basics of chat/text generation: streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/robustness patterns. AE + SE ran a short live demo using the console and a curl SDK example. Customer highlighted latency and compliance constraints (SOC 2, KMS), asked about VPC/on-prem options and cost tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: send sandbox access, security doc, and a small benchmark script.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API quickstart (API key, sandbox)
- Streaming behavior and chunking tradeoffs
- Parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
- Idempotency, retries, and backoff strategies
- Console quick tour: request logs, token breakdown, cost preview
- Compliance and data retention (SOC2, KMS, VPC)

Action items (recap):
- Avery to send sandbox + prompt set
- Devon to prepare benchmark sample
- Priya to consolidate compliance questions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Avery, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Devon, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya (Customer): Good, thanks. Ready to see how this would look in our app.
[00:15] Devon (Redwood SE): Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) box-check onboarding to our hosted sandbox, 2) a short live call to the API showing streaming and params, 3) a console tour of logs and token costs, and 4) Q&A on retries and compliance. Sound good?
[00:32] Carlos (Customer): Yep, especially interested in latency numbers and how streaming looks.
[00:36] Priya (Customer): I'll focus on the compliance bits — SOC 2, KMS, and whether anything hits our VPC.
[00:45] Avery: Great. So first, sandbox access — we'll grant you a scoped API key that expires in 30 days, limits to the sandbox model family. We'll drop that in the email along with a very small prompt set so you can run through it locally.
[01:10] Maya: Nice. Can you show the basic curl example? That's what our backend team will grab first.
[01:15] Devon: Yep, here's a minimal curl for chat generation. We'll stream the response using chunked transfer, so you'll see partial tokens as they arrive. The key bits are: stream=true and then you can consume SSE-like events.
[01:34] Devon: (typing) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -d '{"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize this patient intake note"}]}'
[01:55] Speaker 1: And you get pieces back, so UI can render progressively.
[02:02] Carlos: How often are chunks flushed? Is that per token or per buffer?
[02:07] Devon: Good question. Our runtime flushes in micro-batches — typically every 50-250ms depending on model throughput and sequence length. We chunk on token groups rather than single tokens to avoid a flood of tiny events. So UX feels snappier but not janky.
[02:30] Maya: So if we need very low-latency single token streams for typing indicators, is that supported?
[02:36] Devon: You can tune that a bit by selecting a model variant and enabling low-latency mode, but you'll trade cost/throughput. For most apps we recommend batching slightly and using progressive partials. We also support pushing smaller chunk intervals at the SDK layer.
[02:53] Priya: When you say model variants, do you mean quantized variants on faster hardware? Will data leave our VPC?
[03:00] Devon: For hosted, data flows through Redwood's control plane in managed regions. We log minimal metadata unless you opt-in; payloads are encrypted in transit and at rest with customer-managed KMS options available for dedicated/private deployments. If you require full VPC-on-prem, that's our Private option.
[03:20] Maya: Ok that helps. Let's run the demo.
[03:24] Devon: Alright, I'm going to send a request with stream=true and temperature 0.2 so it's deterministic. Also showing stop sequences to avoid runaway tokens.
[03:35] (Demo noise: short pause, small typing)
[04:02] Devon: You should see the UI receive a start event, partial text, and an end event. That end event includes token counts in the footer for cost preview.
[04:18] Carlos: I see the partials — some words are joined at the boundary, kind of a glueing artifact.
[04:24] Devon: Yeah, occasionally transcribes or concatenates at segment boundaries, that's normal in streamed chunks. The SDK tries to do minimal reassembly.
[04:33] Maya: Any options to reduce that?
[04:36] Devon: Increasing chunk frequency reduces join artifacts but increases message count; the tradeoff is network overhead vs small UX improvements.
[04:45] Avery: On retries — for idempotency we recommend an idempotency key attached to the request. If a client times out, you can retry with the same key to avoid double charging or duplicate stateful outputs.
[04:58] Carlos: Is the key honored across model fallbacks?
[05:02] Devon: Yes, idempotency is tracked at the request layer, not per model. If we fallback, the same idempotency key ensures you don't get two different completions counted as separate attempts.
[05:15] Maya: What about exponential backoff recommendations? Our infra team does 3 retries with jitter.
[05:20] Devon: That's a good baseline. We suggest something like initial 250ms, then exponentially increase to maybe 2s with randomized jitter; avoid tight loops. Also be careful with server errors vs client errors — don't retry 4xx faults.
[05:35] Priya: Can you keep logs for audit? We need to show access logs for SOC 2.
[05:40] Avery: Yes, our Console has per-request logs with headers, token counts, redaction options, and audit trails. For SOC 2 we can provide attestation docs and configure long-term retention as an add-on.
[05:55] Priya: And KMS? Our security team insists on customer-managed keys.
[05:59] Devon: For Private and Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. In hosted, we offer encryption at rest with managed keys by default and optional bring-your-own-key for enterprise contracts.
[06:12] Carlos: On cost — how do streaming partials affect billing? Are partial tokens billed early?
[06:18] Devon: Billing is token-based at completion accounting. Streaming is just a transport; tokens are tallied per response. We also show an estimated cost as you stream via token counter in the SDK.
[06:34] Maya: Can we see the console now?
[06:36] Devon: Yep, switching over. (screen share) Here in the Console you can see a live request, token breakdown, per-route latency percentiles, and the cost preview. The logs let you filter by idempotency key or request_id.
[07:00] (Screen share noise)
[07:20] Maya: The per-token cost graph is handy. Does that reflect batching optimizations?
[07:25] Devon: It does — you'll see lower per-token cost when prefix caching and batching are active. If you have repeated system prompts or shared context, caching can save a lot.
[07:38] Carlos: Tell me more about prefix caching. How is it invalidated?
[07:43] Devon: Prefix or KV caching stores repeated KV cache entries across requests for a specific model/version. It's invalidated on model rollout or if you explicitly purge. There are TTL controls too. We recommend careful prompt design to maximize cache hits.
[07:58] Maya: Does the customer need to change prompts to benefit?
[08:01] Devon: Often small changes help — moving static context to system messages, using placeholders for variables, that kind of thing.
[08:10] Priya: For PHI, we need to ensure we don't persist patient data. How does Redwood handle PII scrubbing?
[08:16] Avery: We offer redaction hooks and the ability to prevent payloads from being stored in logs. For hosted, you can opt-out of request body retention; for Dedicated/Private we can configure no retention at the request layer.
[08:30] Priya: Would that affect troubleshooting?
[08:33] Devon: Some retention helps debugging. We can set a policy to store transient logs for N days with restricted access.
[08:39] Carlos: On a POC, we'd like to run a small benchmark across 1k sample prompts. How would you suggest we set that up?
[08:46] Devon: We'll provide a small script that runs async streaming calls and collects latency percentiles, token counts, and error rates. We'll tune concurrency and batch windows to match your expected workload.
[09:00] Maya: Great. Can you show retry failures?
[09:04] Devon: Simulating a timeout, client can retry with idempotency key. On the Console you'll see a single request record with attempt metadata. If it's a true server failure, the SDK surfaces an error code and you can retry per backoff policy.
[09:20] (short pause)
[09:28] Carlos: Are there limits on concurrency for the sandbox? We don't want to hit throttling while testing.
[09:33] Avery: Sandbox has modest rate limits but we can temporarily raise them for benchmarking work. For production we discuss committed throughput on Dedicated.
[09:44] Maya: Any notes about function calling and structured outputs? We are mapping to internal data models.
[09:50] Devon: Yes, our chat endpoint supports structured responses and function/tool calling. You can define a schema and the model will emit JSON-like outputs. We validate on the runtime to reduce parsing failures — although sometimes the transcription isn't perfect and you need a small post-parse sanitize step.
[10:08] Carlos: Is function calling streamed as well?
[10:11] Devon: Typically the call payload comes at the end of the generation; the streaming layer streams tokens until it emits the function call event. The SDK surfaces that as a structured event.
[10:23] Maya: We're concerned about partial outputs making downstream parsers crash. Any recommendations?
[10:28] Devon: Use a guarded parser: buffer until final event or look for a clear delimiter/JSON fence. If your app needs early partials for UX, have a reconciliation pass when final token arrives.
[10:41] Priya: Security question: do you support SSO/SAML for console access?
[10:44] Avery: Yes, SSO via SAML or OIDC, RBAC role controls, and 2FA for admins. We'll include our admin onboarding doc.
[10:56] Carlos: How do you handle model fallbacks? E.g., if the model times out, do you fallback to a cheaper model?
[11:03] Devon: We have smart routing policies. You can configure graceful fallback to cheaper model variants or to a shorter response width. We also allow canary and A/B rollouts so you can test fallbacks with a small percentage of traffic first.
[11:20] Maya: Let's talk about numeric examples: latency for a 256-token response on typical gen model?
[11:27] Devon: On a well-optimized variant, think 120-250ms per chunk and end-to-end about 400-800ms for 256 tokens depending on concurrency and hardware. For faster low-latency optimized variants, you might see ~200-400ms. These are rough; we'll provide bench scripts.
[11:46] Carlos: If we quantize a model to int8, does that change generation quality?
[11:51] Devon: Slightly—it depends on model architecture. Quantization reduces memory and inference time but may introduce small quality regressions. Redwood Optimize provides recommendations and we can run mixed-precision tests.
[12:05] (Short chuckle)
[12:10] Maya: Any gotchas with streaming through mobile networks?
[12:13] Devon: Mobile has jitter and may break longer-lived connections; use reconnection tokens and idempotency to resume gracefully. Also prefer batched partials to reduce many tiny messages over flaky networks.
[12:28] Priya: For audits, will we get logs that show who accessed which keys and when?
[12:33] Avery: Yes, audit logs with user mapping from SSO and request_id traces. We can push logs to your SIEM or long-term storage if needed.
[12:45] Carlos: On the SDK, what languages are supported?
[12:48] Devon: We support Node, Python, and a lightweight curl flow. There's a Go beta. We'll send links in the follow-up.
[12:57] Maya: Can we white-label the console? Not a hard requirement, but curious for internal teams.
[13:02] Avery: On Dedicated/Private we can offer console theming and restricted views. For hosted, it's standard but you can configure role-based views.
[13:16] Carlos: How do you estimate cost savings from caching and batching?
[13:21] Devon: We provide Optimize suggestions — we'll analyze prompt patterns and recommend batch sizes and quantization. Customers often see 20-60% unit cost reduction depending on workload.
[13:34] Maya: That's compelling.
[13:36] Devon: Quick note on monitoring: console exposes per-route P95/P99 latency, token spend per user, and alerts for quality regressions if you attach an eval suite.
[13:48] Priya: Eval suite — is that something you run with customer prompts?
[13:52] Devon: Yes, Redwood Optimize supports tieing a prompt set to an eval and alerting when generation quality drops after model rollouts or quant changes.
[14:04] Maya: Back to retries — what are the common error codes we should react to?
[14:08] Devon: 429 for rate limits, 502/503 for transient infra errors, 400 for bad requests (don't retry), 401 for auth issues. We add a specific code when a request was rate-limited due to concurrency.
[14:20] Carlos: For 429s, do you return Retry-After?
[14:23] Devon: Yes, we include Retry-After header where possible and a helpful error payload suggesting backoff windows.
[14:31] Maya: Would you be able to share a sample log with redacted PII so our security team can validate retention behavior?
[14:36] Avery: Absolutely, we'll redact and send an example.
[14:41] (brief pause)
[14:49] Devon: One small thing — if you're doing streaming side by side with function calls, it's useful to include a small correlation id in each request so you can trace across services.
[14:59] Carlos: Noted.
[15:02] Maya: Anything else we should be aware of for initial POC?
[15:05] Devon: Keep prompts consistent, save a representative sample of typical requests, and start with a small concurrency baseline then increase to match production pattern. We'll help tune batching windows.
[15:15] Priya: Timeline question: We aim to start POC by 2026-07-20. Is that reachable?
[15:20] Avery: Yes — send us the sample prompts and access needs this week and we'll provision sandbox and a raised rate limit for benchmarking.
[15:30] Carlos: One last thing — on observability, do you offer traces that integrate with Jaeger or OpenTelemetry?
[15:36] Devon: We export trace hooks and logs; OpenTelemetry ingestion is supported for Dedicated and Private; for hosted we can ship logs to your OTEL collector.
[15:46] Maya: Great. That covers most of it.
[15:50] Avery: Let's recap next steps: I'll send sandbox + quickstart, Devon will produce benchmark script, Priya will share compliance questions, and we'll reconvene for POC scoping. Any other items?
[16:03] Maya: No, that's it.
[16:05] Carlos: Thanks all.
[16:07] Priya: Thanks — looking forward to the SOC 2 artifacts.
[16:11] Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email.

(Transcript ends — note: some timestamps are approximate and transcription contains occasional mis-heard words, e.g., "kay vee cash" for KV cache, minor punctuation issues.)
